--- title: "Logistic Regression: Probability, Odds & Classification" description: "Learn logistic regression through a bank-fraud problem: probability, odds, log-odds, sigmoid curves, classification thresholds, precision, recall, F1 and business decisions." author: "MLStation" date: 2026-10-03 categories: [Statistics, Regression, Classification, Machine Learning] draft: false ---
🏦 A $2,400 card transaction arrives at 2:13 AM. Is it fraud?
A bank does not need a prediction such as **0.73 dollars of fraud**. It needs an estimate such as: > **“Given what we know about this transaction, the estimated probability of fraud is 73%.”** Then the bank must make a second decision: > **“Is 73% high enough to block the transaction, request verification, or allow it?”** Those are two different problems. **Logistic regression estimates probability. A threshold converts probability into an action.**
::: {.callout-tip} ## What you will be able to do By the end of this lesson you should be able to: - recognize when a problem is **classification**, not ordinary regression; - explain why a straight-line probability model is problematic; - move between **probability → odds → log-odds**; - interpret logistic-regression coefficients and **odds ratios**; - explain why the sigmoid/logistic curve is needed; - fit a logistic-regression model in Python and obtain fraud probabilities; - explain **TP, FP, TN and FN** in business language; - explain why `0.5` is not automatically the right threshold; - choose a threshold based on **false-negative cost, false-positive cost, recall, precision or F1**; - explain a logistic-regression result to a non-technical stakeholder. ::: Every worked chart follows the same pattern: **Data Simulator → Plot Code → Visible Result**. The two code blocks are folded so you can focus on the visualization and expand the implementation when needed. # 1. The Problem: Detect Fraud, Not a Number Suppose each row is a credit-card transaction. Our target is $$ Y = \begin{cases} 1,&\text{fraud}\\ 0,&\text{legitimate}. \end{cases} $$ Possible predictors include: - transaction amount; - transaction hour; - distance from the customer's usual location; - number of transactions in the previous hour; - whether the merchant is new to the customer; - whether the device is new; - historical customer behavior. For a transaction with feature vector $$ X=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_p), $$ we want to estimate $$ P(Y=1\mid X). $$ Read this as: > **The probability that the transaction is fraudulent, given the information in X.** Here: - $Y$ is the outcome we want to predict; - $X$ is the information available when the decision is made; - $P(Y=1\mid X)$ is a number between 0 and 1.
TRANSACTION FEATURES X → MODEL → FRAUD PROBABILITY → BUSINESS THRESHOLD → ACTION
# 2. Why This Is Classification Regression and classification answer different kinds of questions. | Problem | Target | Example output | |---|---|---| | Linear regression | continuous number | expected monthly spend = $214 | | Logistic classification | category / event | probability of fraud = 0.73 | | Final business decision | action | block / review / allow | A binary classification problem has two outcomes. We encode them as 0 and 1 because that makes the mathematics convenient. The `1` class is usually called the **positive class**. Here: $$ Y=1 \Rightarrow \text{fraud}. $$ “Positive” does **not** mean good. It means the event we are trying to detect. # 3. Why Not Just Use Linear Regression? Linear regression models $$ \hat y = \beta_0+\beta_1x. $$ If we encode fraud as 1 and legitimate as 0, we might be tempted to fit a straight line and call $\hat y$ a probability. But a probability must satisfy $$ 0\le P(Y=1\mid X)\le1. $$ A straight line has no such restriction. ## 3.1 See the problem ### Data Simulator ::: {#98405d63 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng = np.random.default_rng(42) n = 700 amount = rng.gamma(shape=2.0, scale=85, size=n) # Simulated probability of fraud rises with transaction amount. true_logit = -4.2 + 0.012 * amount true_probability = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-true_logit)) fraud = rng.binomial(1, true_probability) linear_vs_logistic = pd.DataFrame({ "amount": amount, "fraud": fraud }) ``` ::: ### Plot Code ::: {#e0f36252 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import numpy as np import plotly.graph_objects as go from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, LogisticRegression X_demo = linear_vs_logistic[["amount"]] y_demo = linear_vs_logistic["fraud"] linear_model = LinearRegression().fit(X_demo, y_demo) logistic_model = LogisticRegression().fit(X_demo, y_demo) grid = np.linspace(0, linear_vs_logistic["amount"].max()*1.12, 350) linear_prediction = linear_model.predict(grid.reshape(-1,1)) logistic_probability = logistic_model.predict_proba( grid.reshape(-1,1) )[:,1] fig = go.Figure() fig.add_scatter( x=linear_vs_logistic["amount"], y=linear_vs_logistic["fraud"], mode="markers", name="Observed transaction", opacity=.18, hovertemplate="Amount: $%{x:.0f}
Fraud label: %{y}" ) fig.add_scatter( x=grid, y=linear_prediction, mode="lines", name="Linear regression" ) fig.add_scatter( x=grid, y=logistic_probability, mode="lines", name="Logistic regression" ) fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dot") fig.add_hline(y=1, line_dash="dot") fig.update_layout( title="Why a Straight Line Is Awkward for a Probability", xaxis_title="Transaction amount ($)", yaxis_title="Fraud label / predicted probability", yaxis_range=[-.25,1.25], height=470 ) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The observed target has only two values: **0 or 1**. Linear regression nevertheless tries to fit a continuous line. For sufficiently small or large values of $x$, the fitted line can predict below 0 or above 1. Those values cannot be probabilities. Logistic regression solves the range problem by transforming a linear score through an S-shaped function that always stays between 0 and 1. # 4. Linear vs Logistic Regression: The Mathematical Contrast ## Linear regression $$ Y \approx \beta_0+\beta_1X+\epsilon $$ and $$ E[Y\mid X=x]=\beta_0+\beta_1x. $$ The right-hand side can take any real value. ## Logistic regression Logistic regression still begins with a linear expression: $$ z=\beta_0+\beta_1x. $$ But $z$ is **not yet the probability**. We transform it: $$ p(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}} = \frac{1}{1+e^{-(\beta_0+\beta_1x)}}. $$ Therefore $$ 0 ### The key idea Logistic regression is still “linear” in an important sense: $$ \beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_px_p $$ is a linear score. The nonlinear logistic function then converts that score into a valid probability. # 5. Probability: What Exactly Does 0.73 Mean? Suppose the model returns $$ P(Y=1\mid X)=0.73. $$ For our problem: $$ P(\text{fraud}\mid\text{transaction information})=0.73. $$ This is **not** the statement: > “This transaction is 73% fraudulent.” A transaction is ultimately fraud or not fraud. A probabilistic interpretation is: > Among transactions receiving comparable model probabilities, a well-calibrated model should see roughly the corresponding fraction become fraud. For example, among many transactions receiving probabilities around 0.80, approximately 80% should be fraudulent if the model is well calibrated. Probability quantifies uncertainty before the outcome is known. # 6. From Probability to Odds People often use probability and odds interchangeably, but mathematically they are different. If an event has probability $p$, its odds are $$ \text{odds}=\frac{p}{1-p}. $$ ## Example: probability = 0.75 $$ \text{odds} = \frac{0.75}{0.25} = 3. $$ This means: > **3 to 1 odds in favor of the event.** For every one expected non-event, there are three expected events under this probability ratio. ## Example: probability = 0.20 $$ \text{odds} = \frac{0.20}{0.80} = 0.25. $$ Equivalent wording: > **1 to 4 odds in favor of the event.** # 7. Probability ↔ Odds Starting with $$ o=\frac{p}{1-p}, $$ solve for $p$: $$ o(1-p)=p $$ $$ o-op=p $$ $$ o=p(1+o) $$ therefore $$ \boxed{p=\frac{o}{1+o}}. $$ So probability and odds contain the same information; they simply use different scales. ## 7.1 Interactive probability-to-odds relationship ### Data Simulator ::: {#9f46075e .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd p_values = np.linspace(.01,.99,199) probability_odds = pd.DataFrame({ "probability": p_values }) probability_odds["odds"] = ( probability_odds["probability"] / (1-probability_odds["probability"]) ) ``` ::: ### Plot Code ::: {#4db42751 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import plotly.express as px fig = px.line( probability_odds, x="probability", y="odds", title="Probability and Odds Are Different Scales" ) fig.add_vline(x=.5, line_dash="dot") fig.add_hline(y=1, line_dash="dot") fig.update_layout( xaxis_title="Probability p", yaxis_title="Odds = p / (1-p)", height=430 ) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Notice: - $p=0.5$ corresponds to odds $=1$; - $p>0.5$ corresponds to odds greater than 1; - $p<0.5$ corresponds to odds less than 1; - odds are not restricted to 0–1. # 8. Why Log-Odds? Odds are positive: $$ 0<\text{odds}<\infty. $$ Taking the logarithm gives $$ -\infty<\log(\text{odds})<\infty. $$ This is exactly the range a linear expression can occupy. Define the **logit**: $$ \operatorname{logit}(p) = \log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right). $$ Logistic regression assumes: $$ \boxed{ \log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \beta_0+\beta_1x } $$ or, with several predictors, $$ \boxed{ \log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_px_p } $$ This is the central equation of logistic regression.
FEATURES X → LINEAR SCORE → LOG-ODDS → ODDS → PROBABILITY
# 9. Deriving the Logistic Function Start with $$ \log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)=z. $$ Exponentiate both sides: $$ \frac{p}{1-p}=e^z. $$ Multiply: $$ p=e^z(1-p). $$ Expand: $$ p=e^z-e^zp. $$ Collect terms containing $p$: $$ p+e^zp=e^z. $$ $$ p(1+e^z)=e^z. $$ Therefore $$ p=\frac{e^z}{1+e^z}. $$ Dividing numerator and denominator by $e^z$ gives $$ \boxed{ p=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}} }. $$ Substitute $z=\beta_0+\beta_1x$: $$ \boxed{ P(Y=1\mid X=x) = \frac{1} {1+\exp[-(\beta_0+\beta_1x)]} }. $$ That S-shaped mapping is the **logistic** or **sigmoid** function. # 10. Why the Logistic Curve Is Needed The linear score $z$ may be: $$ -20,\quad -2,\quad 0,\quad 4,\quad 100. $$ But the sigmoid maps every one of those values into $(0,1)$. Important landmarks: $$ z=0 \Rightarrow p=\frac{1}{2}=0.5. $$ Large positive $z$: $$ p\rightarrow1. $$ Large negative $z$: $$ p\rightarrow0. $$ ## 10.1 Interactive sigmoid: move the intercept and slope Use the sliders to see what $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ do. ```{ojs} //| code-fold: true //| code-summary: "View Interactive Plot Code" viewof beta0 = Inputs.range([-6,6], { value:-2.5, step:.1, label:"Intercept β₀" }) viewof beta1 = Inputs.range([-4,4], { value:1.2, step:.1, label:"Slope β₁" }) sigmoid = z => 1/(1+Math.exp(-z)) sigmoidData = d3.range(-5,5.01,.05).map(x => ({ x:x, probability:sigmoid(beta0 + beta1*x) })) Plot.plot({ height:380, x:{label:"Feature x"}, y:{domain:[0,1],label:"P(Y = 1 | x)"}, marks:[ Plot.ruleY([0.5],{strokeDasharray:"4,4"}), Plot.line(sigmoidData,{ x:"x", y:"probability", strokeWidth:3, tip:true }) ] }) ``` ### Interpret the controls **$\beta_0$ — intercept:** shifts where the curve sits relative to $p=0.5$. **$\beta_1$ — slope:** controls direction and steepness. - $\beta_1>0$: probability rises with $x$; - $\beta_1<0$: probability falls with $x$; - $\beta_1=0$: $x$ contributes no change to log-odds. # 11. What Does a Logistic Coefficient Mean? Suppose $$ \log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \beta_0+\beta_1x $$ and $$ \beta_1=0.7. $$ If $x$ increases by one unit: $$ \text{new log-odds} = \text{old log-odds}+0.7. $$ So the **log-odds increase by 0.7**. But log-odds are not intuitive for most business audiences. Exponentiate: $$ e^{0.7}\approx2.01. $$ Therefore: > A one-unit increase in $x$ multiplies the odds of the positive outcome by approximately **2.01**, holding the other model variables constant. This quantity is the **odds ratio**: $$ \boxed{OR=e^{\beta_1}}. $$ # 12. Odds Ratios: The Most Useful Coefficient Interpretation If $$ \beta_j=0.7, $$ then $$ OR=e^{0.7}\approx2.01. $$ The odds are about **2.01 times as large** after a one-unit increase in $x_j$, all else equal. If $$ \beta_j=-0.4, $$ then $$ OR=e^{-0.4}\approx0.67. $$ The odds are multiplied by 0.67—a reduction of roughly 33%. If $$ \beta_j=0, $$ then $$ OR=e^0=1. $$ No multiplicative change in odds. ::: {.callout-warning} ## Odds ratio is not probability ratio If the odds double, the probability does **not necessarily double**. The probability change depends on the starting probability. ::: # 13. Same Odds Ratio, Different Probability Change Suppose an exposure doubles the odds: $OR=2$. ### Data Simulator ::: {#77b9248e .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd base_p = np.linspace(.02,.90,180) base_odds = base_p/(1-base_p) new_odds = 2 * base_odds new_p = new_odds/(1+new_odds) odds_ratio_demo = pd.DataFrame({ "starting_probability":base_p, "new_probability":new_p }) odds_ratio_demo["probability_change"] = ( odds_ratio_demo["new_probability"] - odds_ratio_demo["starting_probability"] ) ``` ::: ### Plot Code ::: {#edae7374 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import plotly.express as px fig = px.line( odds_ratio_demo, x="starting_probability", y="new_probability", title="A Constant Odds Ratio Does Not Mean a Constant Probability Increase" ) fig.add_shape( type="line", x0=0, y0=0, x1=1, y1=1, line={"dash":"dot"} ) fig.update_layout( xaxis_title="Starting probability", yaxis_title="Probability after doubling the odds", height=440 ) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: For example: - starting at $p=0.10$, doubling odds gives about $p=0.182$; - starting at $p=0.50$, doubling odds gives about $p=0.667$. That is why logistic-regression coefficients are naturally interpreted on the **odds scale**. # 14. A More Realistic Fraud Model Now let us simulate transactions with several useful predictors. We will use: - `amount_100`: transaction amount measured in hundreds of dollars; - `distance_100km`: distance from usual location in hundreds of kilometers; - `new_device`: 1 if the device has not been seen before; - `tx_last_hour`: number of transactions in the previous hour. The model is $$ \log\frac{p}{1-p} = \beta_0 +\beta_1(\text{amount}) +\beta_2(\text{distance}) +\beta_3(\text{new device}) +\beta_4(\text{velocity}). $$ ## 14.1 Simulate and fit ### Data Simulator ::: {#059bc51c .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng = np.random.default_rng(2026) n = 7000 fraud_data = pd.DataFrame({ "amount_100": rng.gamma(2.0,.9,n), "distance_100km": rng.exponential(.55,n), "new_device": rng.binomial(1,.16,n), "tx_last_hour": rng.poisson(.7,n) }) latent_log_odds = ( -4.7 + .42*fraud_data["amount_100"] + .68*fraud_data["distance_100km"] + 1.05*fraud_data["new_device"] + .38*fraud_data["tx_last_hour"] ) fraud_data["true_probability"] = 1/(1+np.exp(-latent_log_odds)) fraud_data["fraud"] = rng.binomial( 1, fraud_data["true_probability"] ) ``` ::: ### Plot Code ::: {#21f91ac6 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import plotly.express as px plot_sample = fraud_data.sample( min(1600,len(fraud_data)), random_state=7 ).copy() plot_sample["amount_dollars"] = 100*plot_sample["amount_100"] plot_sample["class"] = plot_sample["fraud"].map({ 0:"Legitimate", 1:"Fraud" }) fig = px.scatter( plot_sample, x="amount_dollars", y="distance_100km", color="class", symbol="new_device", hover_data=["tx_last_hour","true_probability"], title="Simulated Fraud Problem: Transactions Overlap" ) fig.update_layout( xaxis_title="Transaction amount ($)", yaxis_title="Distance from usual location (100 km)", height=500 ) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Notice the overlap. Fraud does not occur only above one perfect amount or distance. This is exactly why **probability** is useful: the model can represent varying degrees of risk rather than pretending there is a perfect boundary in the raw data. # 15. Fit Logistic Regression in Python ::: {#e03c69ec .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Model-Fitting Code"} from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression features = [ "amount_100", "distance_100km", "new_device", "tx_last_hour" ] X = fraud_data[features] y = fraud_data["fraud"] X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split( X, y, test_size=.30, stratify=y, random_state=42 ) model = LogisticRegression( penalty=None, max_iter=2000 ) model.fit(X_train,y_train) test_probability = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:,1] ``` ::: The important output is not initially `0` or `1`. It is: ```python model.predict_proba(X_test) ``` For binary classification, this returns estimated probabilities for both classes. For a particular transaction we might get: ```text P(legitimate) = 0.27 P(fraud) = 0.73 ``` and the two sum to 1. # 16. Inspect Coefficients as Odds Ratios ### Data Simulator ::: {#01881f69 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Preparation Code"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd coefficient_table = pd.DataFrame({ "feature":features, "coefficient":model.coef_[0] }) coefficient_table["odds_ratio"] = np.exp( coefficient_table["coefficient"] ) coefficient_table = coefficient_table.sort_values( "odds_ratio" ) ``` ::: ### Plot Code ::: {#b56177ea .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import plotly.express as px fig = px.bar( coefficient_table, x="odds_ratio", y="feature", orientation="h", hover_data=["coefficient"], title="Model Coefficients Expressed as Odds Ratios" ) fig.add_vline(x=1, line_dash="dot") fig.update_layout( xaxis_title="Odds ratio = exp(coefficient)", yaxis_title="Feature", height=430 ) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Interpretation depends on each feature's unit. For example, because `amount_100` is measured per **$100**, an odds ratio of 1.5 would mean: > Holding the other included variables constant, each additional $100 multiplies the estimated fraud odds by 1.5. Units matter enormously. # 17. Probability Is Not Yet a Classification Decision Suppose the model gives five transactions: | Transaction | Fraud probability | |---|---:| | A | 0.03 | | B | 0.18 | | C | 0.46 | | D | 0.62 | | E | 0.91 | These are **risk estimates**. To produce labels, choose a threshold $t$: $$ \hat Y = \begin{cases} 1,&\hat p\ge t\\ 0,&\hat p ### Probability model versus decision policy The fitted logistic regression determines the risk score. The **threshold** determines how aggressively the organization acts on that risk. # 18. TP, FP, TN and FN in Plain Business Language After choosing a threshold, every transaction falls into one of four outcomes. | Reality | Bank predicts legitimate | Bank predicts fraud | |---|---|---| | **Legitimate** | **TN** — correctly allow | **FP** — inconvenience a legitimate customer | | **Fraud** | **FN** — fraud gets through | **TP** — correctly flag fraud | ## True Positive — TP Fraud occurred and the model flagged it. **Good:** fraud was detected. ## False Positive — FP Transaction was legitimate but the model flagged it. **Cost:** declined purchase, customer frustration, manual review. ## True Negative — TN Transaction was legitimate and the model allowed it. **Good:** normal customer experience. ## False Negative — FN Transaction was fraud but the model allowed it. **Cost:** financial loss, reimbursement, operational risk. The word **false** means the prediction was wrong. # 19. Threshold Animation: Watch the Confusion Matrix Change ### Data Simulator ::: {#50055b24 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd threshold_rows = [] for t in np.round(np.arange(.05,.96,.05),2): pred = (test_probability >= t).astype(int) tp = int(((pred==1) & (y_test.to_numpy()==1)).sum()) fp = int(((pred==1) & (y_test.to_numpy()==0)).sum()) fn = int(((pred==0) & (y_test.to_numpy()==1)).sum()) tn = int(((pred==0) & (y_test.to_numpy()==0)).sum()) for cell,count in { "TP: fraud caught":tp, "FP: legitimate flagged":fp, "FN: fraud missed":fn, "TN: legitimate allowed":tn }.items(): threshold_rows.append({ "threshold":f"{t:.2f}", "cell":cell, "count":count }) threshold_animation = pd.DataFrame(threshold_rows) ``` ::: ### Plot Code ::: {#6ed88887 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import plotly.express as px fig = px.bar( threshold_animation, x="cell", y="count", animation_frame="threshold", range_y=[0,threshold_animation["count"].max()*1.12], title="Move the Threshold: Every Decision Count Changes" ) fig.update_layout( xaxis_title="Outcome", yaxis_title="Number of test transactions", height=480 ) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Press **Play**. As the threshold rises, the bank becomes more conservative about labeling something fraud. Typically: - fewer transactions are flagged; - false positives decrease; - true positives can also decrease; - false negatives increase. There is no threshold that magically eliminates both types of error when the classes overlap. # 20. Recall: When Missing Fraud Is Expensive Recall asks: > **Of all actual fraud transactions, what fraction did we catch?** $$ \boxed{ \text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP+FN} } $$ The denominator contains **all actual positives**. High recall means few false negatives. For fraud detection, medical screening, safety alerts and some security systems, false negatives can be particularly costly. In such cases, the organization may choose a lower threshold to catch more positives. But that usually creates more false positives. # 21. Precision: When False Alarms Are Expensive Precision asks: > **Of everything we flagged as fraud, what fraction was actually fraud?** $$ \boxed{ \text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP+FP} } $$ The denominator contains **all predicted positives**. High precision means relatively few false alarms among flagged cases. Precision may be especially important when: - every alert requires expensive manual investigation; - customers suffer major friction when flagged; - review capacity is limited; - the positive action itself is costly. # 22. F1: Balance Precision and Recall Sometimes both false positives and false negatives matter and we want one summary that balances precision and recall. The F1 score is the harmonic mean: $$ \boxed{ F_1 = 2 \frac{\text{Precision}\times\text{Recall}} {\text{Precision}+\text{Recall}} } $$ Equivalent form: $$ F_1 = \frac{2TP} {2TP+FP+FN}. $$ F1 is high only when both precision and recall are reasonably high. But F1 does **not** know the dollar cost of fraud, customer friction, staffing constraints or legal requirements. # 23. Interactive Threshold Tradeoff: Precision, Recall and F1 ### Data Simulator ::: {#7f22fb3d .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.metrics import precision_score, recall_score, f1_score metric_rows = [] for t in np.arange(.02,.96,.01): pred = (test_probability >= t).astype(int) metric_rows.append({ "threshold":t, "precision":precision_score( y_test,pred,zero_division=0 ), "recall":recall_score( y_test,pred,zero_division=0 ), "F1":f1_score( y_test,pred,zero_division=0 ) }) threshold_metrics = pd.DataFrame(metric_rows) threshold_metrics_long = threshold_metrics.melt( id_vars="threshold", var_name="metric", value_name="score" ) ``` ::: ### Plot Code ::: {#0aa273d2 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import plotly.express as px fig = px.line( threshold_metrics_long, x="threshold", y="score", color="metric", title="Threshold Is a Business Lever" ) fig.update_traces( hovertemplate="Threshold=%{x:.2f}
Score=%{y:.3f}" ) fig.update_layout( yaxis_range=[0,1.02], xaxis_title="Fraud threshold", yaxis_title="Metric value", height=470 ) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Hover over the curves. A lower threshold generally increases recall because the model flags more transactions. A higher threshold generally increases the strictness required to call something fraud and can improve precision over useful ranges, while recall falls. # 24. How Should a Business Choose the Threshold? There is no universal “correct” threshold. Start with the business consequence.
#### 🛡️ Minimize missed fraud False negatives are very costly. **Emphasize:** recall. Often choose a **lower** threshold.
#### 🚨 Minimize false alarms Investigations or customer blocks are expensive. **Emphasize:** precision. Often choose a **higher** threshold.
#### ⚖️ Balance both FP and FN both matter without a clear asymmetric cost. **Possible summary:** F1. Still inspect the actual errors.
#### 💵 Known business costs Translate TP, FP, FN and TN into money or utility. **Choose:** threshold maximizing expected business value.
# 25. Threshold Selection by Business Cost Suppose, for teaching purposes: - each missed fraud (**FN**) costs $500; - each false alarm (**FP**) costs $12; - catching fraud has no additional modeled loss; - correctly allowing a legitimate transaction has no modeled loss. Then $$ \text{Cost}(t) = 500\,FN(t) + 12\,FP(t). $$ This is not a universal fraud-cost model. It is an example of converting business consequences into a threshold objective. ### Data Simulator ::: {#87b6f39f .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd business_rows = [] for t in np.arange(.02,.96,.01): pred = (test_probability >= t).astype(int) truth = y_test.to_numpy() tp = ((pred==1)&(truth==1)).sum() fp = ((pred==1)&(truth==0)).sum() fn = ((pred==0)&(truth==1)).sum() tn = ((pred==0)&(truth==0)).sum() cost = 500*fn + 12*fp business_rows.append({ "threshold":t, "TP":tp, "FP":fp, "FN":fn, "TN":tn, "business_cost":cost }) business_threshold = pd.DataFrame(business_rows) best_business_row = business_threshold.loc[ business_threshold["business_cost"].idxmin() ] ``` ::: ### Plot Code ::: {#84026a51 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import plotly.express as px fig = px.line( business_threshold, x="threshold", y="business_cost", title="Choose a Threshold from Business Consequences" ) fig.add_vline( x=float(best_business_row["threshold"]), line_dash="dash", annotation_text=( "Lowest simulated cost: " f"{best_business_row['threshold']:.2f}" ) ) fig.update_layout( xaxis_title="Fraud threshold", yaxis_title="Simulated error cost ($)", height=450 ) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: This makes the logic explicit: > The threshold is not chosen because 0.5 “looks mathematically natural.” It is chosen because a particular operating point best supports the decision objective. ::: {.callout-important} ## Important correction to a common simplification It is not generally true that businesses “mostly maximize recall.” Some applications strongly prioritize recall; others prioritize precision, capacity, expected cost, safety, customer experience, or a constrained combination. The metric should follow the **consequence of the errors**. ::: # 26. A Three-Zone Policy Can Be Better Than One Hard Threshold Real systems do not always need only two actions. A bank might use: ```text p < 0.10 → allow automatically 0.10 ≤ p < 0.60 → request verification / review p ≥ 0.60 → block or escalate ``` Probability is valuable precisely because it supports **graded decisions**. The model can rank risk while the business chooses multiple action regions. # 27. What About Accuracy? Accuracy is $$ \text{Accuracy} = \frac{TP+TN} {TP+TN+FP+FN}. $$ It can be misleading for rare events. Suppose only 1% of transactions are fraud. A useless model that predicts **“legitimate” for every transaction** achieves: $$ 99\%\text{ accuracy}. $$ But: $$ \text{Recall}=0. $$ It catches no fraud. For imbalanced classification, always ask what the metric is rewarding. # 28. Precision–Recall Curve: See Many Thresholds at Once Instead of selecting one threshold immediately, inspect the available precision–recall tradeoff. ### Data Simulator ::: {#09789c95 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Preparation Code"} import pandas as pd from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve pr_precision, pr_recall, pr_threshold = precision_recall_curve( y_test, test_probability ) pr_data = pd.DataFrame({ "recall":pr_recall[:-1], "precision":pr_precision[:-1], "threshold":pr_threshold }) ``` ::: ### Plot Code ::: {#41f2d18b .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import plotly.express as px fig = px.line( pr_data, x="recall", y="precision", hover_data={"threshold":":.3f"}, title="Precision–Recall Tradeoff Across Thresholds" ) fig.update_layout( xaxis_range=[0,1.02], yaxis_range=[0,1.02], height=470 ) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Hover over the curve to inspect thresholds that produce different operating points. # 29. Probability Quality: Calibration A classifier can rank transactions well but still give poor numerical probabilities. A well-calibrated model should approximately satisfy: > Among transactions assigned probability near 0.20, about 20% are actually fraud. This matters if probabilities drive: - expected-loss calculations; - pricing; - resource allocation; - risk tiers; - decision thresholds based on cost. ## 29.1 Calibration plot ### Data Simulator ::: {#65c51665 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Preparation Code"} import pandas as pd from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve observed_rate, mean_predicted = calibration_curve( y_test, test_probability, n_bins=10, strategy="quantile" ) calibration_data = pd.DataFrame({ "mean_predicted_probability":mean_predicted, "observed_fraud_rate":observed_rate }) ``` ::: ### Plot Code ::: {#73535ea7 .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import plotly.graph_objects as go fig = go.Figure() fig.add_scatter( x=calibration_data["mean_predicted_probability"], y=calibration_data["observed_fraud_rate"], mode="lines+markers", name="Model" ) fig.add_scatter( x=[0,1], y=[0,1], mode="lines", name="Perfect calibration", line={"dash":"dash"} ) fig.update_layout( title="Do Predicted Probabilities Match Observed Frequencies?", xaxis_title="Mean predicted fraud probability", yaxis_title="Observed fraud rate", xaxis_range=[0,1], yaxis_range=[0,1], height=470 ) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: # 30. How Logistic Regression Learns The model needs coefficients that make observed outcomes probable. For observation $i$, let $$ p_i=P(Y_i=1\mid X_i). $$ Because $Y_i\in\{0,1\}$, its Bernoulli likelihood contribution can be written compactly: $$ P(Y_i=y_i) = p_i^{y_i}(1-p_i)^{1-y_i}. $$ For independent observations: $$ L(\beta) = \prod_{i=1}^n p_i^{y_i} (1-p_i)^{1-y_i}. $$ Taking logs turns products into sums: $$ \ell(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ y_i\log p_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-p_i) \right]. $$ Logistic regression chooses coefficients that maximize this log-likelihood, or equivalently minimize the negative log-likelihood / log loss.
### Why this loss makes sense If the true outcome is fraud ($y=1$), the model is rewarded for assigning high $p$. If the true outcome is legitimate ($y=0$), the model is rewarded for assigning high $1-p$. Confidently wrong probabilities are penalized heavily.
# 31. One Transaction from Beginning to End Suppose a fitted model is $$ \log\frac{p}{1-p} = -4.0 + 0.5x_1 + 0.8x_2 + 1.1x_3, $$ where: - $x_1$ = amount in hundreds of dollars; - $x_2$ = distance in hundreds of kilometers; - $x_3$ = new-device indicator. For a $400 transaction: $$ x_1=4. $$ Suppose it is 200 km from the usual location: $$ x_2=2. $$ and it uses a new device: $$ x_3=1. $$ Then $$ z = -4 + 0.5(4) + 0.8(2) + 1.1(1). $$ $$ z=0.7. $$ This is the log-odds. Convert to odds: $$ \text{odds}=e^{0.7}\approx2.01. $$ Convert to probability: $$ p = \frac{2.01}{1+2.01} \approx0.668. $$ So the estimated fraud probability is approximately 66.8%. Now the business rule acts. At threshold 0.50: $$ 0.668\ge0.50 \Rightarrow \text{flag fraud}. $$ At threshold 0.80: $$ 0.668<0.80 \Rightarrow \text{do not flag}. $$ **Nothing about the fitted probability changed. Only the decision policy changed.** # 32. How to Explain a Logistic Regression Result A good explanation has three levels. ## Level 1 — Probability > “The model estimates a 67% probability of fraud for this transaction.” ## Level 2 — Feature / odds interpretation > “Holding the other modeled variables fixed, a one-unit increase in this predictor multiplies fraud odds by $e^{\beta_j}$.” ## Level 3 — Decision > “Our current operating threshold is 40%, so this transaction is sent for review.” Do not collapse these into one statement. ```text MODEL INTERPRETATION ≠ PROBABILITY INTERPRETATION ≠ BUSINESS DECISION ``` # 33. Common Mistakes ## Mistake 1: “Logistic regression predicts 0 or 1.” More precisely, logistic regression estimates probabilities/scores; a decision rule converts them into class labels. ## Mistake 2: “A coefficient of 0.7 means probability rises by 70%.” No. It means log-odds increase by 0.7 per unit, and odds are multiplied by $e^{0.7}$. ## Mistake 3: “Odds ratio 2 means probability doubles.” No. Probability change depends on the starting probability. ## Mistake 4: “0.5 is the correct threshold.” It is a common default, not a universal business optimum. ## Mistake 5: “High accuracy means good fraud detection.” Not with severe class imbalance. ## Mistake 6: “High recall is always best.” Only when the value of catching positives justifies the false-positive burden and other consequences. ## Mistake 7: “Probability 0.8 automatically means 80% of such cases are positive.” That interpretation requires adequate calibration on the relevant population. # 34. Probability Is the Center of the Classification Story Logistic regression is valuable because it separates **uncertainty estimation** from **action**.
X ↓ LINEAR SCORE z = β₀ + βᵀX ↓ LOG-ODDS ↓ exp() ODDS ↓ o/(1+o) PROBABILITY P(Y=1|X) ↓ threshold / policy CLASSIFICATION OR BUSINESS ACTION
Probability enables several different uses: ### Ranking Who is riskier? ```text 0.91 > 0.72 > 0.28 ``` ### Binary classification Is probability above a chosen threshold? ### Multiple action tiers Allow, verify, review, block. ### Expected value Combine probability with financial consequences. ### Communication Explain uncertainty rather than pretending every prediction is certain. # 35. A Compact Decision Guide | Business question | What to examine | |---|---| | “How likely is fraud?” | predicted probability | | “How does x change risk?” | coefficient + odds ratio | | “Catch as much fraud as possible” | recall + FN | | “Reduce false alarms” | precision + FP | | “Balance precision and recall” | F1 + actual error counts | | “Choose an operating policy” | threshold curves | | “Errors have dollar values” | expected business cost/value | | “Can we trust 0.8 as 80%?” | calibration | | “Fraud is rare” | precision–recall behavior + class balance | # 36. Final Mental Model
✨ Logistic regression does not begin with classification. It begins with probability.
The model learns a linear relationship on the **log-odds scale**, converts it to a probability with the **logistic function**, and only then does the organization choose how that probability becomes a decision.
Remember the chain: $$ \boxed{ X \rightarrow \beta_0+\beta^TX \rightarrow \log\frac{p}{1-p} \rightarrow p \rightarrow \text{threshold} \rightarrow \text{action} } $$ # Summary - Fraud detection is a **binary classification** problem because the target is fraud/not fraud. - Linear regression is poorly suited to modeling a probability directly because a line is unbounded. - Logistic regression models $$ \log\frac{p}{1-p} = \beta_0+\beta^TX. $$ - The sigmoid converts any real-valued score into a probability between 0 and 1. - Odds are $$ \frac{p}{1-p}. $$ - A coefficient $\beta_j$ changes log-odds additively. - $e^{\beta_j}$ is the corresponding **odds ratio** for a one-unit predictor increase, holding other included predictors fixed. - The predicted probability and the final class decision are different objects. - Thresholds control the balance between TP, FP, TN and FN. - Recall emphasizes catching positives and reducing FN. - Precision emphasizes reliability of positive flags and reducing FP. - F1 balances precision and recall, but does not encode actual business costs. - The best threshold depends on the real consequence of errors. - Calibration asks whether numerical probabilities correspond to observed event frequencies. - Probability is what makes logistic regression useful not only for classification, but for ranking, risk estimation, tiered actions and business decisions. **Next:** *Bayesian Statistics — Learning by Updating*
